clue.text: Report damage, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sharp bang, like the report of a gun
second meaning: a split or fracture in something

explanation.surface: Someone files a written account of harm done, say to a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Report' looks like a verb meaning to tell officials, but here it is the noun for a loud bang.
explanation.definitionFit: A gunshot's sharp noise and a fracture in glass are both called by this one short word.

clue.text: It's stalked in the country to provide food

definitions.text: It's stalked in the country to provide food

parts.words: It's stalked in the country to provide food
parts.note: surface reading: game hunted in rural areas for the pot
setter's reading: having stalks, the field of a cereal crop grown for grain

explanation.surface: Deer are stalked across the countryside to put meat on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stalked' reads as hunted, but it means bearing stalks.
explanation.definitionFit: A cornfield is farmland planted with a cereal crop on tall stalks, harvested for food.

clue.text: One of the London Bells?

parts.note: surface reading: a church bell from the 'Oranges and Lemons' rhyme
setter's reading: the three Brontë sisters' shared pen surname, each with a male first name, one of which is also a London district

explanation.surface: A question about one of the city's famous peals of church bells.
explanation.walkthrough: Anne Brontë wrote under the pen name Acton Bell; Acton is also a district of west London, so it is a London Bell.
explanation.definitionFit: The name was Anne Brontë's pseudonym, shared with a west London suburb.

clue.text: Fancy dish gives thrill to playwright

parts.note: a kick is a buzz of excitement
George Bernard Shaw, the Irish dramatist

explanation.surface: An elaborate meal excites a dramatist.
explanation.definitionFit: A kickshaw is an old word for a fancy, dainty dish, from French quelque chose.

clue.text: Took off without direction being fixed

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense of outside means one word wraps around the other

parts.note: to take someone off is to mimic them
a point of the compass gives a direction

explanation.surface: A plane departed with no heading settled on in advance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Took off' suggests a plane leaving, but it means mimicked; 'without' is used in its old sense of outside.
explanation.definitionFit: An appointed time or place is one that has been settled or arranged beforehand.

clue.text: One of a pair on the wagon takes drink about ten

definitions.text: One of a pair on the wagon

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the drink goes round the other piece

parts.note: ale is beer
the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: A teetotaller who is on the wagon still has a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the wagon' means abstaining from alcohol, an idea the drink in the wordplay plays against; here it is a literal cart.
explanation.definitionFit: A four-wheeled cart has two axles, the rods on which each pair of wheels turns.

clue.text: Sharpen up the consumer in Hampshire

definitions.note: a place in Hampshire; the definition names where it is

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means the letters run upwards, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to strop a razor is to sharpen it on a leather strap
the mouth is what consumes food

explanation.surface: A knife-grinder sharpens tools for a customer in Hampshire.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampshire is a county on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Portsmouth is the naval port city on the Hampshire coast of southern England.

clue.text: Injure two after motorway upset

indicators.note: 'after' places the first-named piece behind the second, fixing the order they are joined in
in a down clue something upset is turned upside down, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's first motorway, with 1 read as I
two of a kind make a pair

explanation.surface: Two people are hurt following a crash on the motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: To impair something is to damage or weaken it, a close synonym of injure.

clue.text: Marine bad hat takes girl in charge

indicators.note: something bad is spoilt or out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the three letters, rearranged
a lass is a girl
i/c is the abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A soldier in the marines who is a bad lot takes charge of a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marine' looks like a noun for a soldier, but it is the adjective meaning of the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Thalassic means relating to the sea, from the Greek word thalassa.

clue.text: Trick Dawkins was skilful at

definitions.meaning: second meaning: Jack Dawkins is the Artful ... in Oliver Twist

explanation.surface: A sporting star named Dawkins was good at a particular trick.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Dawkins is the real name of Dickens's pickpocket the Artful Dodger.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodge is a sly trick, and a dodger is someone practised at it, as Dickens's character was.

clue.text: Engineers curtail broadcast in network

definitions.note: adjective phrase: arranged like a net

indicators.note: seed that is broadcast is scattered widely, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
the word's seven letters, rearranged

explanation.surface: Army engineers cut short a radio transmission across their communications network.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curtail' looks like a deletion signal, but it is the fodder for the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Reticular describes something formed like a net or mesh, so it means arranged as a network.

clue.text: Cloth with soft face turned back

parts.note: p (piano) means soft in music

indicators.note: something turned back faces the other way, so these letters are read from right to left

parts.note: a clock's face is its dial

explanation.surface: A fabric with a soft surface has had its edge folded back.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaid is a woollen fabric woven in a tartan pattern, a kind of cloth.

clue.text: Polish, or another nationality, say

indicators.note: 'say' asks us to speak the word, so a word that sounds the same is wanted

parts.note: a person from Finland is Finnish, a nationality other than Polish

explanation.surface: Someone is described as Polish, or perhaps of some other nationality.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes 'Polish' look like a nationality, but it is the verb meaning to put a final shine on.
explanation.definitionFit: To give something its final finish is to polish it, as with a coat of varnish on wood.

clue.text: Judge is abroad, with one companion

parts.note: est is French for 'is'
the Roman numeral for one
a mate is a friend or companion

explanation.surface: A judge is travelling overseas with a single companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like a noun for a magistrate, but it is the verb meaning to reckon.
explanation.definitionFit: To estimate is to form a rough judgement of a size, value or amount.

clue.text: Postpone reception — he won't travel

parts.note: to stay proceedings is to postpone them
an at-home is a reception held in one's own house

explanation.surface: A party is put off because one guest refuses to make the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: An at-home is an old-fashioned name for a party or reception given at the host's house.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay-at-home is a person who prefers to stay put and avoids going away.

clue.text: Lineage we might expect of a dentist

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ancestry, as in a person of noble descent

definitions.text: we might expect of a dentist
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the pulling of a tooth

explanation.surface: Someone muses on what sort of family background a dentist would come from.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's extraction is their descent or origin; a dentist's extraction is the removal of a tooth.

clue.text: Pay the Post Office, so to speak

definitions.text: Pay the Post Office, so to speak

parts.note: surface reading: settle a bill at the post office counter
setter's reading: the Post Office ran Britain's phone service, so to call someone was in effect to pay it in order to speak

explanation.surface: Someone goes to settle up at the post office.
explanation.walkthrough: Until 1981 the British Post Office ran the national phone network, so every call was money to it; 'so to speak' is a pun on speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: To telephone is to make a call, which earned the Post Office a fee when it ran the phone service.

clue.text: Mount part of gigantic ladder

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a mountain in Thessaly, Greece
second meaning: in Greek myth the giants piled one mountain on another to climb to heaven, Pelion on top

explanation.surface: Someone climbs onto one rung of an enormous ladder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' looks like the verb to climb, but it is a mountain. The phrase 'heaping Pelion on Ossa' comes from that myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Ossa is a mountain in Thessaly which the giants used as a step in their stack of peaks reaching for heaven.

clue.text: Money obtained from letter? .

parts.note: surface reading: cash that arrives in the post
setter's reading: a letter is one who lets or permits, so what such a person grants is money given by permission

explanation.surface: Cash has turned up enclosed in a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'letter' here is someone who lets, that is, allows; a regular sum handed over is named after allowing.
explanation.definitionFit: An allowance is a set sum of money given regularly, such as pocket money from a parent.

clue.text: Remoulded retreads must be checked

indicators.note: something remoulded has been shaped anew, so these letters are formed into a new order

parts.note: the eight letters, rearranged

explanation.surface: Re-moulded tyres have to be inspected for safety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'checked' suggests inspected, but it means halted.
explanation.definitionFit: Growth or progress that is arrested has been stopped or held back.

clue.text: Stupid view of the foreign learners

parts.note: du is French for 'of the'
L is a learner driver's plate; two learners make LL

explanation.surface: Someone holds a low opinion of the foreign students.
explanation.walkthrough: 'view' does no work in the wordplay; it only builds the surface picture of a dim opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull can mean slow-witted or lacking intelligence, as in a dull pupil.

clue.text: Sounds like his new article is violently emotional

indicators.note: a new version is a remade one, so these letters are put in a fresh order
what something sounds like is how it is spoken, so a word with that sound is wanted

parts.note: spelt differently but spoken the same
the word's seven letters, rearranged

explanation.surface: A writer's newly published article sounds wildly overwrought.
explanation.walkthrough: 'article' looks like it should give A or THE, but all its letters are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Hysterical describes someone overcome by uncontrolled, extreme feeling such as panic or wild laughter.

clue.text: Wood on sides round a sort of masonry

parts.note: ash is a hardwood tree

indicators.note: 'round' means surrounding, so the outer pieces go around what follows

parts.note: left and right are the two sides
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wooden frame fits around a stonework structure.
explanation.walkthrough: The A in the clue is used twice: once inside L and R, and again as part of the definition 'a sort of masonry'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashlar is masonry of finely dressed square stones laid in regular courses.

clue.text: A quiet river situation appears suitable

parts.note: taken as written
p (piano) means quiet in music
the Po is the great river of northern Italy
a site is a location or situation

explanation.surface: An estate agent says a peaceful riverside location looks just right.
explanation.definitionFit: An apposite remark or choice is apt, well suited to the occasion.

clue.text: Grotesque action, nothing less

indicators.note: 'less' means without, so the named letter is taken away

parts.note: taken as written
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A bizarre performance, no less.
explanation.walkthrough: With O removed, the remaining letters must still be shuffled, yet the clue has no separate anagram word; 'Grotesque' has to do double duty as definition and the hint to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Antic as an adjective means bizarre or fantastic, like a clown's grotesque capers.

clue.text: Give some bribes to weak characters

indicators.note: 'some' means only a portion is taken, a run of letters inside the words that follow

parts.note: a run of letters straddling the three words
surface padding: the letters are the characters being taken

explanation.surface: Someone hands out bribes to people of feeble moral fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans the end of 'bribes', all of 'to' and the start of 'weak'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bestow something is to present it as a gift or honour, a formal way of giving.

clue.text: Sign for a book, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a symbol or indication
second meaning: a voucher exchangeable for goods

explanation.surface: An author is asked to autograph a book.
explanation.walkthrough: A book token is a gift voucher redeemable at a bookshop.
explanation.definitionFit: A token is an outward sign of something, and also a voucher, as in a gift exchangeable for a book.

clue.text: Letters held by northern banks

definitions.meaning: first meaning: more than one of the twentieth letter, spelt out
second meaning: a river in the north-east of England, contained between its banks

explanation.surface: Correspondence is being kept by banks in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' suggests money, but these are riverbanks; the Tees flows past Middlesbrough in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The letter T is spelt out as tee, and the Tees is a river in northern England flowing between its banks.

clue.text: Mythical giant fish

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a monster of Scandinavian folklore
second meaning: to angle by trailing a baited line behind a boat

explanation.surface: A legendary enormous fish of the deep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fish' looks like a noun qualified by 'giant', but it is a verb on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Trolls are giants or ogres of Norse legend, and to troll is to fish with a line dragged through water.

clue.text: Bit of test submitted to, and passed

parts.note: in cricket a Test match is made up of overs of six balls
an exam submitted to is one taken

explanation.surface: A student sat part of an exam and got through it.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test is an international cricket match; an over is a set of six balls bowled from one end.
explanation.definitionFit: A car that has been overtaken has been passed by another on the road.

clue.text: How sad to reduce number of tigers

parts.note: a tiger was an extra yell tacked onto a round of cheers
to have fewer of something is to have less

explanation.surface: Someone laments a plan to cut the population of big cats.
explanation.walkthrough: Old American usage: 'three cheers and a tiger' ended with a growled shout called a tiger, so tigers are cheers.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cheerless is gloomy and dispiriting, lacking any brightness or comfort.

clue.text: Stupid compact

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it suggests a foolish agreement, but the two words are separate meanings of one adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A dense person is thick-headed, and dense material is tightly packed with little space inside.
